#2890. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#2885. Procter & Gamble's Dividend Has Survived 26 Recessions. Here's What $10,000 Now Earns in Yearly Dividend Income.

P&G has paid a dividend through 26 recessions and raised it for 70 straight years. Here's what $10,000 earns today, and why the streak looks safe.

Since Procter & Gamble (PG -1.02%) was incorporated in 1890, the National Bureau of Economic Research has counted 26 U.S. recessions. The Panic of 1893. The Great Depression. The 1970s, twice. The dot-com bust, the financial crisis, the pandemic. Through all of it, the company that makes Tide and Pampers mailed a dividend check every single quarter, and for the last 70 years each annual check has been larger than the one before. That makes this ticker a Dividend King, a designation for companies that have increased annual dividends for at least 50 consecutive years.

All of this is not a marketing line. It is the closest thing the stock market has to a promise kept. The question for anyone buying the stock today is whether a promise that old still has something behind it.

Procter & Gamble raised its quarterly dividend to $1.0885 per share in April, a 3% increase. That works out to $4.35 a year. With the stock trading near $166, the yield is about 2.6%, so a $10,000 investment buys roughly 60 shares and produces about $265 a year in dividend income.

That is not a number that changes anyone's life. What changes a life is what the number does over time. P&G's dividend has risen more than 60% over the past decade, and if the next 10 years look like the last 10, that $260-ish becomes something north of $430 a year on the same shares, without buying another one. The point of owning P&G is not the yield you get today. It is the yield you get on the price you paid, 10 and 20 years from now, from a company that has never once broken the streak.

A 136-year dividend history is really a statement about management discipline. Every Procter & Gamble CEO since Benjamin Harrison was U.S. president has viewed the dividend as the one thing they were not allowed to touch, which forces a certain conservatism in how the company borrows, acquires, and spends. P&G's own language in the April release says it plainly: many shareholders "rely on the steady, reliable income earned with their investment in P&G."

That matters now, because things are getting harder. On its October earnings call, P&G said it expects roughly $1.4 billion in higher commodity, energy, and freight costs this fiscal year, and that oil above $100 a barrel would be an "increasing headwind." Core gross margin fell 150 basis points in the quarter. This is the operating environment in which weaker consumer companies cut their payouts; Campbell's (CPB -1.28%) and Flowers Foods (FLO -5.49%) both did this year.

The encouraging part is that demand is holding. First-quarter organic sales rose 4%, with growth in all 10 product categories and all six regions,  most of it coming from volume rather than price. That is the healthiest kind of growth a consumer company can have, because it means people are buying more Tide and Crest, not just paying more for the same amount. New CEO Shailesh Jejurikar, who took over in January, also added Thorne, a supplements brand, pushing P&G into a wellness category it had never entered. The company maintained its full-year outlook despite the cost pressure, and the stock posted its best day in more than a year after the report.

The harder part is margin. P&G built its reputation on raising prices without losing customers, and that lever is nearly spent; pricing contributed almost nothing to the quarter. The company is leaning on productivity programs to absorb the cost squeeze, and management has been candid that fiscal 2027 "won't be a straight line."

To me, yes, and the reason is structural rather than sentimental. P&G pays out about two-thirds of its earnings as dividends, which leaves a cushion even in a bad year. It generates more than $15 billion in annual profit from products that people buy in a downturn, sometimes in smaller sizes, but rarely not at all.

A $10,000 stake earning $260 a year will not make you rich. But it has a better chance than almost any stock on the market of still paying you, in larger amounts, when the next recession comes and goes.

#2881. Could Buying Palantir Stock Today Set You Up for Life?

The company's strong leadership in AI software has propelled the stock to life-changing returns since late 2020.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR +3.48%) has already changed lives for investors who bought in early. Since the company's direct listing in 2020, shares have soared by more than 1,500%. That would have turned $10,000 into roughly $162,000 in roughly five years.

But can buying Palantir stock now still set you up for life? Unfortunately, math is not on your side. Despite the company's blistering growth, the stock's next 1,500% will probably take far longer. Here's why.

Few companies can match the explosive growth Palantir is achieving. It generated just over $2.3 billion in total revenue in the third quarter of 2026, growing 96% year over year and 20% over the prior quarter. Palantir has been posting eye-popping growth for a few years now, which is how the stock has produced such high returns.

That success has already made Palantir, at a market cap of $412 billion, one of the world's largest companies. It's a hefty valuation for a company of Palantir's revenue base, even with that rampant growth rate. At its current price, shares trade at 55 times sales, making it one of Wall Street's more expensive names.

But even if Palantir sustains that valuation, it's going to be difficult for the stock to continue rising as it has. Even another 100% will push it to near a $1 trillion market cap. There aren't many stocks worth $1 trillion or more, and those that are all generate significantly more revenue.

So it's unrealistic to expect Palantir to rise another 1,500% anytime soon. It will probably take years of prolonged success.

Of course, Palantir can still set you up for life with returns of 100% to 300%. The catch is that you need to invest a bit more than you would for a stock that grows 1,500%. That leads to the question of whether it's wise to risk an enormous capital investment in just one stock.

Such a large investment is difficult for most diversified portfolios. It's probably wiser to lower your expectations for Palantir stock than to take a big risk by putting too much of your portfolio into one company.

The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has eroded in the early sessions following the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats regained control of the Senate and the House of Representatives. This shift could lead to a more aggressive regulatory stance toward the AI industry.

An extended sell-off would let a bit of air out of the stock. If that happens, long-term investors who believe in the company's ongoing momentum can recapture some of the stock's upside at more attractive entry prices.

#2878. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

#2876. Bloom Energy Stock Fell 16% on the Same Day 2 Giant Data Center Deals Named It. Is It a Buy?

Only one of the two deals is new business. Is the stock's drop an opening?

Bloom Energy (BE +3.42%) turned up in two big data center announcements on Nov. 5. NTT DATA said it had agreed to deploy 900 megawatts of the fuel cell maker's onsite power across data center projects around the world.

And Alphabet's Google said Bloom would build the fuel cells for a 702-megawatt plant powering its first data center in Wyoming, a $17 billion project.

The stock had a bad day anyway. Shares ended at $167.52, off around 16%, amid worries that rising opposition to new data centers after the Nov. 3 midterms might slow the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

The growth stock is still up over 90% this year. But it now sits about 52% below the $345.85 record close it set on June 22.

How much new business did Bloom win on Nov. 5? Less than the headlines may suggest, because just one of the two deals is new. I think the other still matters, though, and the stock looks much more reasonably priced than it did in October.

Google won't buy the fuel cells itself. American Electric Power plans to invest around $4 billion in the 702-megawatt project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, the utility said on Oct. 14. It'll sell the plant's output to Google under a 20-year power purchase agreement, and it expects the plant to be fully running by late 2028.

The fuel cell order came months earlier. In January, an AEP subsidiary agreed to buy solid oxide fuel cells for around $2.65 billion for a plant near Cheyenne. The purchase used most of an option for 900 extra megawatts under AEP's 2024 supply deal with Bloom.

For a sense of scale, that one order is worth over half of Bloom's full-year revenue forecast of $4.4 billion to $4.6 billion for 2026.

So, Google's news didn't add to Bloom's orders. The fuel cells were bought in January, and AEP had already named Google as the plant's customer in October.

That still means something, I think. A fuel cell order backed by a 20-year power contract with Google looks more likely to become revenue on time than one linked to an unnamed buyer.

NTT DATA's deal is the new business, and the companies called it Bloom's biggest international project so far. NTT's data center arm plans to use the fuel cells as its main power source, with the relationship meant to reach gigawatt scale across its global portfolio.

What the release didn't say matters, too. It gave no dollar value, no project locations, and no timeline beyond first shipments starting in 2027. This deal shouldn't show up in Bloom's 2026 revenue, and Bloom hasn't said how much of it falls in 2027 or later.

But 900 megawatts is a lot of fuel cells -- nearly a full year of output at the 1 gigawatt of annual production capacity Bloom's Fremont, California, plant had going into 2026. The company planned to double that capacity by year-end.

Bloom needs deals like this, because its quarter-to-quarter growth slowed sharply in the third quarter. Second-quarter revenue of $1.07 billion was 42% above the first quarter's $751 million. Third-quarter revenue then climbed 16% sequentially to $1.24 billion, up 138% year over year. And October's raised outlook (management's third raise this year) implies a sequential gain of 9% to 25% in the fourth quarter.

That's still strong growth. Keeping it up into 2027 and 2028, though, depends on deals like NTT DATA's moving from announcement to shipment.

Based on the midpoint of management's adjusted earnings forecast for 2026 ($3.10 to $3.40 a share), Bloom stock cost around 52 times earnings at its Nov. 5 close. The same forecast had it at around 67 times earnings at the $217.77 close on Oct. 22. On next year's expected earnings, shares now trade at around 31 times earnings.

Still, 52 times earnings is a premium price. It assumes Bloom keeps growing quickly well past this year.

But Bloom landed a big new deal on Nov. 5 as its shares got much cheaper.

Of course, a slower U.S. data center build-out might delay some deliveries. And October's weak spot hasn't gone away. Bloom's operations burned $27 million in cash in the third quarter, mostly because it booked revenue faster than it could bill customers for it.

Is Bloom stock worth buying after a 16% one-day drop? I'd consider buying some shares at this price, a few at a time. And I'd maybe add more when billing catches up with revenue.

#2868. Phoenix bent but never broke against the Rockets

Saturday night's victory over the Houston Rockets was easily the Phoenix Suns' best win of the season. Granted, they've only won three games through their first eight, but this one felt different. Phoenix continued its recent trend of putting together quality first quarters, something that has become increasingly important given how frequently this team has found itself playing from behind. When the Suns fall into an early deficit, players tend to press, forcing the issue offensively and abandoning the systems and schemes designed to put them in positions to succeed.

But Saturday night presented a different kind of adversity. After building a lead that reached as many as 19 points, the Suns completely unraveled in the second quarter. They managed a miserable 12 points, shot 3-of-11 from beyond the arc, and apparently decided to let amber be the color of their energy as Houston closed the half on a 22-3 run to erase the deficit entirely (that's a 311 joke). What had been a commanding Phoenix advantage was suddenly a tie game heading into the locker room.

And that's where things got interesting. Throughout the second half, we witnessed a collection of quality performances from different players on both ends of the floor. There were timely offensive contributions, defensive adjustments, and moments when individual effort helped stabilize a team that had every reason to start questioning itself. By the time the final buzzer sounded, the Suns had earned a 102-99 victory over one of the NBA's most potent offenses.

That's right. For the first time this season, Phoenix held an opponent under 100 points. And that opponent happened to be the Houston Rockets.

That accomplishment alone makes this victory impressive, but what stands out even more is how the Suns responded after their complete second-quarter meltdown. When you surrender a 19-point advantage in such a short period of time, it's easy to fold. It's easy to begin doubting yourself, questioning whether you have the personnel, discipline, or defensive capability to stop the opponent standing across from you. We've seen that uncertainty creep into this team's play far too often through the opening weeks of the season.

Saturday night, however, was the first time we truly witnessed the mental toughness and fortitude that defined this team a season ago. The Suns refused to let one disastrous quarter dictate the outcome of the game. They regrouped, stood tall, and collectively found a way to shut down a Houston offense that had been operating like a well-oiled machine. In doing so, they earned, in every sense of the word, their third victory of the season.

What a ride Jeremy Sochan has had, and the new season is just getting underway. After nearly four seasons with the San Antonio Spurs, he was waived and signed with the Knicks, picking up a championship ring when New York beat the Spurs in the 2026 Finals.

After New York, it appeared Sochan was spending the 2026-2027 season in Portland, but was waived after four preseason games. The Polish-American power forward declared for the G-League draft and one week later was chosen first overall by the Texas Legends.

Here he is earlier this week in his first press conference as a member of the Legends.

"I think the way I grew up, my family, my parents; it's always been like that. I could look at it negatively (the Portland situation). But when I look back at that situation, I think the two months I was there, I grew a lot. I was healthy throughout the whole training camp, preseason and open gym. So I think that was a blessing. When we got into preseason games, the minutes I got I think I used them to the best of my ability. I had good games. So what would be the point of being negative and angry for getting waived? Of course, you can look at it as that's the NBA and I have a contract. But at the same time I have good momentum. So, why would I hold weight on something that I can't control? And instead, be in this moment and do what I can do and keep that momentum going."

According to Marc Spears, Sochan originally found out he was being waived by the Spurs through another player:

"I thought I was going to be there for the rest of the season at least. And a few days after the trade deadline, it's funny. #2858. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#2855. Moderna: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its proprietary software is built into the cancer drug itself, creating a front-end design moat that rivals may struggle to replicate.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 6, 2026, Moderna (MRNA +5.27%) announced an upgraded full-year revenue framework alongside positive Phase 3 clinical trial data for its individualized cancer therapy. The biotechnology company is demonstrating that its messenger RNA (mRNA) drug-delivery platform can expand beyond respiratory vaccines to high-value oncology treatments while controlling operating costs. Three key takeaways from management explain how this business transition affects long-term shareholders.

Moderna and partner Merck generated positive Phase 3 results for Intismeran autogene, an individualized neoantigen therapy (INT) designed to train a patient's immune system against specific tumor mutations. The clinical trial showed that adding the vaccine to Keytruda, an established immunotherapy, lowered relapse risks in skin cancer patients compared to Keytruda alone.

Management raised its 2026 full-year revenue growth target to between 15% and 25%, up from prior expectations of up to 10% growth. Expanded international supply agreements and stable domestic uptake for mNEXSPIKE, Moderna's updated COVID-19 vaccine, drove the outlook increase while cash spending dropped 10% year over year.

Moderna considers the bioinformatic algorithm that identifies patient neoantigens -- the unique protein mutations on cancer cells -- an integral component of its therapeutic product rather than standard software. This proprietary digital system creates a competitive moat by linking patient sequencing data directly to individualized manufacturing.

Vaccine commercialization is accelerating across global markets, and executive leaders are emphasizing expense control alongside expanding commercial opportunities.

Moderna's long-term enterprise value relies on establishing high barriers to entry through individualized manufacturing algorithms and multiyear supply agreements. Management remains focused on advancing late-stage oncology trials, obtaining international regulatory approvals, and executing Biologics License Applications -- the formal requests for commercial drug clearance -- to sustain commercial momentum.

#2852. SpaceX's Starlink Could Build a Nationwide Cell Network. Here's What Investors Need to Know

SpaceX is looking to build a terrestrial cellular network.

Space Exploration Technologies' (SPCX +8.62%) future hinges on its ability to scale its AI division, which comprises more than 90% of the company's total anticipated growth runway. But for now, the space company's Starlink satellite network is generating the most cash flow.

Starlink already provides millions around the world with high-speed internet connectivity. The division has also begun selling bandwidth to terrestrial cellphone networks when users are outside a service zone.

Long term, however, Starlink appears poised to launch its own cellular network. Here's what investors should know.

According to Axios, "SpaceX has spent billions on spectrum and struck a multiyear agreement with Qualcomm to build a 5G network." The outlet also reports that SpaceX may be interested in acquiring an existing terrestrial cellular network to jump-start its user base and acquire additional frequency rights.

SpaceX estimates that the entire Starlink opportunity long-term is valued at roughly $1.6 trillion. Based on the valuations of major U.S. carriers, a successful cellular division could capture several hundred billion dollars of that estimated total value.

But building a terrestrial network won't just be about consumer cellphone plans. As Axios points out, a "combined satellite and terrestrial network could eventually serve autonomous vehicles, delivery drones, robots, and other connected devices. That could give SpaceX opportunities beyond the already competitive consumer wireless market."

In short, building a complementary terrestrial cellular network would help SpaceX not only launch a consumer cellphone offering, but also target the rest of its estimated $1.6 trillion connectivity opportunity. It will likely take years for this process to fully play out, but it's key for SpaceX to realize all of its growth opportunities and justify its lofty valuation.

#2842. Against Oklahoma City, the Wizards were the bug

Oklahoma City Thunder broadcaster Michael Cage summed up this game perfectly: "In this game, sometimes you're the bug, and sometimes you're the windshield." In this one, the Wizards were in the role of the bug.

Washington was no match for the Thunder. Oklahoma City took control early and the Wizards had no answer for their athleticism, execution, and swarming defensive presence.

The Wizards converted just 29.6% of their field goal attempts, including 7-43 from three-point range. That's 16.3%. Which is bad. Very bad.

Positives for the Wizards were scarce. Among them — Alex Sarr grabbed 14 rebounds in 28 minutes. Bub Carrington shot 3-3 from deep. Bilal Coulibaly defended Shai Gilgeous-Alexander pretty well in the first quarter — SGA had two points on o-3 shooting when Coulibaly left the game. He immediately started scoring and finished the game with 30 points and 9 assists.

For Washington, it's a third consecutive loss — their first three-game skid of the season. Before the game, head coach Brian Keefe talked with reporters about the team figuring out their formula for success. The team would be wise not to over-index on this game. It was a bad result, and the team looked awful.

Despite missing Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren (in some order, their second and third best players), OKC is a special case. It's a championship-level team with something to prove. The Wizards need to learn to compete at that level, and the lesson of their last three games is that they're still not close.

That's not the end of world 10 games into the season. But they need to internalize that lesson and do the work to become competitive against high-level opponents.

Kudos to the OKC stadium operations team — when the Wizards starters got introduced, they played Harry Potter theme music. Good job.

The Wizards entered the game with the NBA's second best "in the paint" field goal percentage (62.2%). The Thunder had the NBA's second best defensive paint FG% (holding opponents to just 50.2%). Safe to say OKC won that battle.

In the first quarter, the Wizards ran a pick-and-roll option out of a horns set for AJ Dybantsa. He had a choice of going left or right. It didn't go great — he ended up battling his way into a mid-ranger, which he missed. The set was good, though.

Tre Mann got real minutes for the first time this season. He looked pretty good — quick, aggressive, athletic. I'd like to see more.

Jotted during the second quarter (could have been jotted anytime) — OKC defenders switch HARD.

Another second quarter note — OKC was doubling Trae Young to get the ball out of his hands. The other Wizards weren't able to take make plays, in part because OKC defenders hustled back to their matchups and rotated so perfectly.

I thought maybe the Wizards had a chance of making things respectable — a thought that disappeared when I saw their possession of the second half. It was a pick-and-roll for Kyshawn George, who got caught in no-man's land. The only teammate who cut was Coulibaly, who didn't get free. That should have triggered a cascade of movement, but the other guys stood around until George was forced to take a difficult shot, which he missed.

The Wizards tried a small-ball lineup in the second half. It got shredded by Aday Mara and the Thunder.

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

#2822. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#2821. Lululemon Athletica vs. On: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Lululemon's steady profits stand in contrast to On's blistering revenue growth, but its declining sales raise a key question.

Investors face a choice between established market leadership and high-growth momentum when comparing Lululemon Athletica (LULU -0.88%) and On (ONON -0.48%). Both companies are vying for dominance in the competitive athletic category.

Lululemon is known for its high-end yoga and technical apparel, whereas On has built its reputation on innovative running footwear. This comparison explores their financial health and market positioning to determine the better long-term pick.

Lululemon Athletica designs and sells technical athletic apparel, footwear, and accessories through an omni-channel model. It reaches customers via more than 800 company-operated stores and a robust e-commerce platform across multiple countries.

The company also leverages wholesale channels by partnering with fitness studios and university retailers. This diversified approach helps it maintain high brand visibility and reach a loyal customer base in the apparel sector.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $11.1 billion, representing revenue growth of approximately 4.9% compared to the prior year. Net income for the period was roughly $1.6 billion.

On develops and distributes premium performance sports products, primarily focusing on its innovative footwear technology. As of the end of 2025, the company operated nearly 70 retail locations worldwide and maintains a strong presence through wholesale partners and its direct-to-consumer e-commerce platform.

Its growth strategy emphasizes global expansion, with a significant retail footprint already established in China. The company relies on its high-performance brand image to attract runners and lifestyle consumers willing to pay a premium price.

In FY 2025, revenue reached roughly $3.7 billion, which reflects impressive revenue growth. Net income for the fiscal period was approximately $246 million.

Lululemon Athletica faces several legal and operational hurdles, including multiple class action lawsuits regarding its financial guidance and brand health. The company is also navigating a management transition at the CEO position. External factors like changes in U.S. tariff policy and supply chain concentration in Asia add further uncertainty. Increased competition from rivals that can quickly imitate technical designs may also pressure its historical brand premium.

On must navigate the challenges of scaling a global logistics network while competing against much larger footwear giants like Nike. Maintaining its premium pricing and brand exclusivity becomes more difficult as the company moves into broader wholesale distribution. Inventory management is a critical risk, as any miscalculation in demand could lead to heavy discounting that hurts net margin. The company also remains sensitive to shifts in consumer discretionary spending across its primary markets in Europe and North America.

Lululemon currently offers a more conservative valuation profile, while On carries a premium multiple that reflects its significantly faster revenue growth trajectory.

Each company provides slightly different offerings, but both are generally in the fitness and activewear segment. Both are considered premium brands and can struggle when consumers tighten their budgets. They may like Lululemon pants or shoes from On, but in tighter times, a consumer may just trade down to a different brand with similar items at lower prices. That said, there's still opportunity to find the right stocks in that sector of the market. According to Fortune Business Insights, the global sportswear market is expected to grow from $235 billion in 2026 to $402.5 billion by 2034.

For this battle, I would choose On for one main reason. The reason is that On is more in the opening stretch of its journey, with less than 100 stores. In comparison, Lululemon ended 2025 with 811 stores, and it's transitioning into a more mature company, looking for what its next stage will look like. Also, you can see it in the sales growth. For the second quarter of 2026, On reported that revenue increased 13.5%, while Lululemon reported net revenue decreased by 4%. Ultimately, anyone interested in On should dig into its financials a bit more before considering it as an investment. Still, based solely on a comparison with Lululemon, I'd rather own On at this moment in time.

#2817. 3 Super Growth Stocks to Buy Hand Over Fist If the Stock Market Crashes

One of these stocks is up 265% over the past year -- and its shares don't seem wildly overvalued, either.

Is a market crash imminent? No one knows for sure, but on the day that I'm writing this, the S&P 500 has pulled back by more than 4% -- a big move. Will that continue? We can't know. A pullback of some sort, potentially triggering a recession for a while, is likely at some point, though, because crashes and corrections simply happen every few years or so -- and several indicators are pointing to a crash.

You shouldn't keep any short-term money (funds you expect to need within the coming five, if not 10, years) in stocks, and if you're following that guideline, you should plan to just ride out any downturns. Better still, downturns present great buying opportunities. Here are some growth stocks to consider buying the next time the market corrects.

Eli Lilly (LLY -0.79%), home to popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Mounjaro and Zepbound, has been a blockbuster performer, averaging annual stock price gains of nearly 40% over the past five years. (It's up some 57% over the past year, too, as of early November.) It's no surprise, then, that the stock seems somewhat overvalued, with a recent price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 14.7, above the five-year average of 13.3.

You could invest in it now if you plan to hold for many years, but buying after a market pullback will get you in at a lower price and boost your eventual gains.

The company is performing quite well lately, posting a 39% year-over-year increase in revenue for its third quarter while management upped its projections for the full year. It's true that its pricing has gone down a bit, but that was more than made up for by increased volume. Lilly also faces competition, but it remains a major player in the GLP-1 world and is expanding there, too, such as via its oral drug Foundayo.

Of course, Lilly is not solely a GLP-1 specialist. It's also home to Kisunla for Alzheimer's disease, Ebglyss for eczema, and cancer drug Jaypirca, among other medications.

Micron Technology (MU +5.12%) is a major semiconductor company specializing in memory and storage chips. It's been posting boffo gains lately, as it supplies memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) processing, and AI has been growing briskly. Micron's shares have averaged annual gains of 47% over the past decade, much of that due to outsize gains in recent years. Over the past year, for example, shares are up 265%!

Should you invest in Micron? It's certainly tempting, especially for long-term investors. The shares are even down some 26% over the past month (as of early November). That's due in large part to competition from Chinese company CXMT, as well as worries that the AI and data center build-out might take a breather. But such worries may be overblown, with rival chipmaker SK Hynix seeing a memory shortage persisting through 2030.

Meanwhile, Micron shares seem reasonably valued or a bit undervalued at recent levels, with a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 5, below the five-year average of 11. If you hold out for a market pullback (which may happen this year but could happen later), you'll be getting in at an even more attractive point.

Then there's Nvidia (NVDA +2.77%), the semiconductor titan with a recent market value of $4.4 trillion. It actually seems attractively valued right now, with a recent forward P/E ratio of 13, well below the five-year average of 33. So you might buy into it now if you like what you see after further research.

Shares have averaged annual gains of 52% over the past 15 years, and 65% over the past three years. Growth is likely to continue, though possibly at somewhat slower rates. Nvidia is the biggest supplier for AI model training and inference, and it's expanding its scope to include software, networking, and services.

The company will be reporting its third-quarter results on Nov. 17, and Nvidia has guided for revenue to more than double year over year. If it outperforms, shares could get a nice boost, and if it doesn't, well, arguably, its shares are already down in expectation of that.

Take a closer look at any of these stocks that interest you, and as long as you plan to hold for years, you might buy some shares sooner rather than later. Otherwise, add them to your watch list.

The Houston Rockets hit their first losing streak of the season on Saturday night, as they let the Suns run all over them to start, battled back, but then couldn't close out the game.

For their last loss against Minnesota, it was a ghost of last season — execution — that was a main culprit. This time, it was shooting. The Rockets couldn't hit the broad side of the barn, and you have to credit the Phoenix defense. They looked like the fresher team in the fourth quarter, when they shot 11-for-22 from the field, while the Rockets were only 10-for-27. In fact, for the game, Houston shot just 38 percent from the field, while allowing the Suns to shoot 48 percent. You're not gonna win many that way.

In fact, the only Rocket player with a semi-decent game was Jabari Smith Jr., who continues to break out this season offensively. Smith went for 15 points on 7-for-12 shooting, 9 rebounds, 2 assists, 3 steals and a block, though he was just 1-for-4 from deep. Still, Smith was the only Rockets player who could hit some shots outside of Fred VanVleet. FVV went for 16 points, 3 rebounds, and 4 assists while shooting 6-for-12 from the floor and 4-for-9 from deep. VanVleet mostly played a clean game with zero turnovers, however, you want to see greater assist numbers, and with the offense stuck in the mud most of the game, you also want to see a greater impact from a distribution standpoint. But when no one is hitting shots…

Kevin Durant led the Rockets in scoring with 21 points, and he also had 10 boards and 3 assists, but he shot just 5-for-14 for the game, including 1-for-5 in a decisive fourth quarter that the Rockets lost. Alperen Sengun had 15 points, but he was just 5-for-16 from the field. Houston's bench also shot just 6-for-25 for the game, including a combined 3-for-16 from Tari Eason and Reed Sheppard. Reed played just 13 minutes in this one, and it is increasingly appearing he is the odd man out in the rotation, especially if the three isn't falling — and it wasn't on Saturday at just 2-for-6 from deep.

The Suns were led by Devin Booker's 24 points, while former Rocket Jalen Green had 16 points and 6 assists, and other former Rocket Dillon Brooks had 11 points and 4 boards while hitting 3 triples.

Houston falls to 7-3 on the season, and after a fast start (just like last year), some warts are starting to appear (just like last year), including late-game execution, overall shooting, and rotation management, again many of the same issues as last season. Nevertheless, the team is currently on a 57-win pace, but with the Western Conference wide open this year, you'd like to see the Rockets looking a little tighter.

#2815. Sixers visit Bulls for second meeting in Sunday matinee

The Philadelphia 76ers have one more game on this road trip before they head home, visiting the Chicago Bulls on Sunday afternoon.

This is the second time in under a week the Sixers and Bulls are meeting, with the Sixers winning their first foray 126-107 back on Monday. With the Bulls going into that contest 1-5, some may have expected the then 6-1 Sixers to have handled that game with ease… but it took until the final few minutes for Philadelphia to finally pull away from Chicago. Since then, the Bulls have dropped to 1-7 on the season, and come into Sunday on a six-game skid.

Looking at the injury reports, Joel Embiid is currently probable for Sunday's contest due to plantar fasciitis management. Not sure if it was what was bothering him on Friday, but he certainly seemed off in that one to say the least. And the hits just keep coming at the center position for Philadelphia with Adem Bona ruled out for a second consecutive game due to a cervical spine sprain. This may mean that — for better or worse —there's more pressure on Embiid to play even if he isn't 100% right now. The only other injury note for the Sixers are that Dominick Barlow (back) remains out.

For the Bulls, there is some mystery around who may be playing center for them tomorrow as well. Nic Claxton is currently listed as questionable after being sidelined to start the season with a hamstring strain. Him being listed as questionable is a step toward the direction of the Bulls' starting center possibly taking the floor against the Sixers. Jalen Smith, who has been starting at the five in Claxton's absence, is probable with a left finger sprain. Also for Chicago, Tobe Awaka is questionable while Zach Collins and Dailyn Swain are out.

The Bulls will have the rest advantage this afternoon as they haven't played since Wednesday for some unknown reason. Who am I to question the wisdom of the NBA schedule makers?

Earlier this week, the Sixers utilized a widespread effort across their starters to get the job done against the Bulls. All five starters scored in the double-digits, and three scored more than 20 points each. It was an especially impressive night from VJ Edgecombe, who shot 9-for-12 from the floor and 2-for-4 from behind the arc for 21 points. Tyrese Maxey had a 26-point, 11 assist double-double, Jaylen Brown added a 25-point, 11-rebound double-double, and LeBron James posted 15 points and nine assists — some of which were just incredible displays of playmaking.

I'm a big believer in "if it ain't broke, don't fix it". One of the things the Sixers did exceptionally well in that contest was getting out in transition on a clinical level. A shot would go up on the defensive end, James would be ready to rebound as Edgecombe or Maxey preemptively charged up the floor. A few incredible, quarterback-level passes from James and the Sixers enjoyed the benefits of taking the easy buckets as they came.

That last part is my advice for the Sixers tonight: don't make it harder than it needs to be. Take the easy buckets out in stride when you can get them. Don't let the Bulls grab offensive rebound after offensive rebound for second chance points. Don't rely on one player to do all the heavy lifting. Spread the floor and the ball, and don't turn it into a battle to the end with a team that is objectively worse. If you can, get a lead big enough that even Nick Nurse gives the starting five a little rest toward the end.

Coming off just their second loss of the season, one can imagine the Sixers coming into Sunday with a strong desire to right the ship. Right there with them is a Bulls squad that is desperately trying to find their footing this season and may have their starting center back in the mix. Regardless, this is one that the Sixers really should win, barring any major changes to the injury reports pregame.

But we all know how well "should" goes in the NBA.

The Sixers and Bulls tip off at 3:30 p.m. ET.

#2814. Magnite vs. Pinterest: Which Media Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

One operates the ad-tech backbone for streaming; the other has built a massive online platform. Their financial profiles and risk exposures also tell very different stories.

As digital advertising shifts toward streaming and social commerce, choosing between Magnite (MGNI -0.47%) and Pinterest (PINS -4.19%) requires a close look at where marketing dollars are moving today.

Magnite serves as the technical backbone for publishers looking to sell ad space, while Pinterest provides a visual search environment where users actively look for inspiration and products. Comparing these two companies helps investors understand the different ways to play the ongoing evolution of the digital ad market.

Magnite provides a sell-side advertising platform for publishers and media owners in the media stocks landscape. As the largest independent player in this space, it helps content creators monetize their inventory across connected television, mobile, and desktop. The company maintains critical partnerships with providers like LG Ad Solutions and Telly, allowing programmatic buyers, including The Trade Desk, to access premium video inventory.

In FY 2025, Magnite reported revenue of nearly $714 million, representing a growth rate of approximately 6.9% compared to the previous year. The company achieved a net income of roughly $144.6 million during this period. This is an increase from the net income of approximately $22.8 million reported in FY 2024, reflecting an expansion in its net margin to roughly 20.3%.

Looking further into the financials, Magnite has total cash of $392.8 million and total debt of $411.9 million. Its operating cash flow for the 12-month trailing period is nearly $300 million.

Pinterest operates a visual discovery and shopping platform that now serves approximately 661 million monthly active users. Unlike traditional social media, the platform focuses on curation, making it highly attractive to advertisers in the retail and consumer packaged goods sectors. By integrating shopping features directly into its pins, the company has transformed from a simple image board into a performance-driven marketing channel.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $4.2 billion, which was an increase of nearly 15.8% over the previous year. The company reported a net income of roughly $416.9 million for the year. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 9.9%, which followed a net margin of roughly 51% in FY 2024 when the company benefited from significant tax adjustments and valuation changes.

For a quick glimpse at the financials, Pinterest has $1.4 billion in total cash and $1.2 billion in total debt. Its operating cash flow for the 12-month trailing period is $1.3 billion.

Pinterest faces significant competition for user attention and advertising budgets from Amazon, Meta Platforms, Alphabet, and smaller rivals like Snap (SNAP -2.55%) and Reddit (RDDT +1.38%). The company is currently involved in a securities class action lawsuit related to previous advertising disclosures. Furthermore, Pinterest remains vulnerable to changes in mobile operating systems that limit tracking capabilities, which can make it harder for advertisers to measure the effectiveness of their campaigns.

Pinterest appears to be more of a value, according to traditional metrics.

Pinterest has built up an impressive monthly user base. And there is something to be said for building your own network and controlling that user base. But Pinterest is caught between being a social media site and an advertiser, whereas Magnite's value is more straightforward. Also, between the two, Magnite is more of a growth stock, whereas Pinterest is seeking more stability, with its stock price down 30% over the last 12 months. In comparison, the Magnite stock price is up 81.3% over the same period.

Analysts also have a more favorable outlook on Magnite: of the 18 analysts who rate Magnite, 89% rate it a buy, with 11% rating it a hold. In comparison, the view is more split on Pinterest. Of the 42 analysts who rate PINS, 50% rate it a buy and 50% a hold.

As a growth stock, Magnite could be hit particularly hard if there were a slowdown in the economy. And heading into 2027, we're seeing concerns about an artificial intelligence bubble and mixed signals about the economy's strength. Still, between the two, I would rather own Magnite as a long-term position because of its sales growth opportunities.

#2813. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#2811. Palantir vs. Snowflake: The AI Sell-Off Is Exposing a Critical Difference for 2027

Palantir and Snowflake continue to deliver impressive growth, but soaring AI expectations and renewed market volatility are putting their valuations under scrutiny.

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has fueled remarkable growth across the technology sector, but the recent sell-off has Wall Street reconsidering how much that growth is worth. For investors looking toward 2027, the pullback presents an opportunity to reassess two leading enterprise AI players: Palantir Technologies (PLTR +3.48%) and Snowflake (SNOW +2.35%).

Both of these companies are benefiting from growing AI adoption, but their distinct business models, financial performance, and valuations present nuanced investment opportunities.

Palantir develops software platforms that help government agencies and businesses integrate complex datasets, improve decision-making, and deploy artificial intelligence. Its Gotham, Foundry, and Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) products serve customers ranging from the U.S. military to commercial enterprises.

In fiscal 2025, Palantir generated $4.5 billion in revenue, an increase of 56% year over year. Net income reached approximately $1.6 billion, representing a profit margin of 36.5%. More recent results demonstrate accelerating growth. In the third quarter of 2026, revenue surged 96% to $2.3 billion, while U.S. commercial revenue climbed 148%. Notably, U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time, highlighting the company's expanding presence in the private sector.

At the end of 2025, the company carried virtually no debt, with a current ratio of approximately 7.1x. Free cash flow reached $2.1 billion during the year, providing substantial flexibility to fund continued expansion. However, stock-based compensation totaled approximately $684 million, representing 32% of operating cash flow, which could introduce potential shareholder dilution despite the company's strong cash generation.

Snowflake operates a cloud-based data platform that enables businesses to store, manage, and analyze information across multiple cloud environments. Its consumption-based pricing model allows customers to pay for the computing resources they use, while partnerships with Amazon (AMZN -0.35%), Microsoft (MSFT -0.99%), and Alphabet (GOOGL +0.78%) (GOOG +0.78%) support its global reach. As businesses increasingly incorporate artificial intelligence into their operations, Snowflake's platform plays an important role in making enterprise data accessible for AI applications.In fiscal 2026, Snowflake generated approximately $4.7 billion in revenue, an increase of 29% year over year. Still, it was unable to turn a profit and reported a net loss of $1.3 billion, representing a negative profit margin of roughly 28%. However, more recent results demonstrate continued growth. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue increased 35% to $1.55 billion, while product revenue climbed 37%.

At the end of fiscal 2026, its debt-to-equity ratio stood near 1.2x, while its current ratio was approximately 1.3x. The company generated $1.1 billion in free cash flow, but stock-based compensation totaled $1.6 billion, exceeding operating cash flow.

One of the key risks for Palantir comes from its reliance on large government and enterprise contracts, where lengthy sales cycles and customer concentration can create revenue uncertainty. In addition, its involvement in sensitive defense and surveillance operations also introduces regulatory and reputational risks.

Top risks for Snowflake include intense competition and a consumption-based revenue model that makes growth sensitive to customer spending. Not to mention, ever-growing cybersecurity threats introduce operational and regulatory risks.

Snowflake offers a lower P/S ratio, measuring price against sales over the past twelve months, while Palantir is cheaper relative to future earnings estimates via its Forward P/E.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

From a valuation standpoint, neither stock is cheap. Palantir trades at 103 times forward earnings, while Snowflake commands an even higher multiple of 131 times. Snowflake is considerably cheaper on a price-to-sales basis, at 18.9 times sales compared with Palantir's 54.5 times, but its continued losses and path toward sustained GAAP profitability are less certain.The key difference is that Palantir has demonstrated a stronger ability to turn growing AI adoption into profits. Its latest quarterly revenue surged 96%, driven by accelerating commercial demand, while its strong balance sheet and minimal debt provide considerable financial flexibility.Looking ahead to 2027, Palantir is my preferred buy, although its valuation gives me pause. Investors are paying a substantial premium for future growth, leaving little room for disappointment if the company falls short of expectations. Ultimately, both stocks carry lofty valuations, and the recent sell-off doesn't automatically make either a bargain.

RJ Fulton has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Palantir Technologies, and Snowflake. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#2809. Milwaukee Bucks vs. Boston Celtics Preview & Game Thread: Revenge game

The Milwaukee Bucks are looking to halt a five-game slide as they take on Eastern Conference heavyweight Boston Celtics, who beat Milwaukee by seven points without Jayson Tatum on Wednesday. The Bucks and Celtics seem to be moving in entirely different directions. After a slow start to the season, Boston is surging at 7-2 and challenging the Sixers for the No. 1 spot in the conference. Meanwhile, the Bucks are 1-8 and face a daunting schedule that could easily extend their losing streak. On the plus side, Milwaukee's youth looks strong—Brayden Burries looks great, and Nate Ament is taking exciting developmental steps—and despite the horrible record, we've been treated to some really exciting Tyler Herro performances. What else can we look forward to?

The Boston Celtics have been on a tear recently. They've won their last two—Wednesday's back-and-forth win over Milwaukee and a blowout Friday win over the Charlotte Hornets—and have claimed five wins in their last six games. They're second in the East, half a game behind the Sixers, and, with the addition of Paul George, look like an early title contender.

Moreover, aside from some glaring valleys—namely the season opener against the Detroit Pistons—Jayson Tatum has performed at an MVP level so far. His highlights include a 36-point near-triple-double against the Knicks, a 40-point outburst against the Nets (that included a game-winning shot), and a recent 34-point near-triple-double against the Hornets in just 29 minutes. But it hasn't been all Tatum; Paul George has averaged just under 20 PPG on solid shooting, Derrick White remains the ultimate glue guy, and Neemias Queta anchors one of the league's best defenses. In three words: Boston is back. In four words: Boston is really back. In five words… you get it.

Bogoljub Markovic: Out (G League assignment)

Chris Cenac Jr: Out (G League assignment)

Derrick White is always fun to watch, especially as he eases into a more offensively significant role in Boston. White is a connective guard with a high basketball IQ and solid playmaking, but he is also an elite defender who can shut down on the perimeter. Against Milwaukee on Wednesday, the veteran guard scored 24 points on 7/18 shooting and added seven assists. White scored 18 points on 6/10 shooting with five assists and four boards in Boston's demolition of the Hornets. He'll be a key point-of-attack defender who could frustrate a Milwaukee backcourt prone to turnovers. Watching Brayden Burries go up against one of his draft comparisons in White will also be interesting.

Who: Milwaukee Bucks (1-8) vs. Boston Celtics (7-2).

The Celtics lead by at least 15 points by the end of the first quarter. The Celtics led Milwaukee 28-14 by the end of the first frame in their last meeting, and that was without Tatum. Boston's aggressive defense could give the streaky Bucks a tough time, and the C's have the star power on offense to make this a one-sided affair.
